React 19 itself is fine per peers, but the library is React-only — unusable in a Vue/Nuxt codebase.

Browser support (README-confirmed): 'Safari and Firefox only partially support the effect (displacement will not be visible)'. Code UA-sniffs Firefox and sets filter:null (backdrop blur+saturate+bezel only); Safari gets the filter property but WebKit does not apply SVG filter chains to backdrop-filter output, so displacement and chromatic aberration silently vanish — Safari renders frosted blur, saturation, bezel rings, sheen, shadows only. Also SSR-unsafe: navigator/window accessed during render (Remix issue #21).

Cost: npm unpacked 180KB / 11 files; each bundle (ESM or CJS) ~70KB with ~41KB of embedded base64 maps that gzip poorly (~40KB gz realistic). Runtime: 3-pass SVG displacement over a backdrop-filtered layer is GPU/CPU heavy (frame-drop reports, issue #3); every mousemove triggers a full React re-render rebuilding inline gradient strings; shader mode runs an O(width*height) main-thread pixel loop on mount/resize; element size tracked via getBoundingClientRect + window resize only (no ResizeObserver).

Layout model: forces position relative/absolute with top/left 50% + translate(-50%,-50%) and renders 5-7 absolutely-positioned SIBLING layers (over-light x2, glass, bezel x2, hover x3) that must stay size/transform-synced — placement in normal flow is painful (issue #20); over-light and content layers use Tailwind utility classnames (bg-black, opacity-20, mix-blend-overlay, text-white) that must exist in the host build.
designRules: Glass substrate token: backdrop-filter: blur(var(--glass-blur, 6px)) saturate(var(--glass-saturate, 140%)); blur range 4-14px (12px base over light backgrounds). This is the effect's load-bearing layer and works in Chromium AND Safari (-webkit-backdrop-filter).

Separate warp layer from content: the filtered/displaced surface is an absolutely-positioned empty layer (inset:0) behind a z-index:1 content layer — children must never sit inside the filtered element, so text stays sharp while the backdrop warps.

Bezel ring utility: overlay with padding:1.5px; background:linear-gradient(...); mask: linear-gradient(#000 0 0) content-box, linear-gradient(#000 0 0); mask-composite: exclude (-webkit-mask-composite: xor) — paints the gradient only on a 1.5px rim without borders.

Double-pass bezel: stack two identical rings, one mix-blend-mode:screen at opacity ~0.2 (additive glint) and one mix-blend-mode:overlay (contrast-reactive) so the rim reads on both light and dark backdrops.
Bezel micro-shadows: 0 0 0 0.5px rgba(255,255,255,0.5) inset + 0 1px 3px rgba(255,255,255,0.25) inset (top-lit glass lip) + 0 1px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.35) (contact shadow).

Bezel gradient recipe: linear-gradient(135deg, transparent 0%, rgba(255,255,255,0.12) ~33%, rgba(255,255,255,0.4) ~66%, transparent 100%); optionally drive the angle (135 + mouseX*1.2 deg) and stop alphas from pointer position via CSS custom properties for a live specular.

Depth shadow tokens: 0 12px 40px rgba(0,0,0,0.25) on dark backdrops; 0 16px 70px rgba(0,0,0,0.75) over light ('overLight' variant), paired with a black 20% dimming overlay + a black mix-blend-overlay layer and halved displacement.

Sheen states: radial-gradient(circle at 50% 0%, rgba(255,255,255,0.5-1) 0%, transparent 50-100%) overlay layers with mix-blend-mode:overlay; opacity 0 rest -> 0.4-0.5 hover -> 0.8 active; press feedback scale(0.96); transition all 0.2s ease-out.

Displacement enhancement (Chromium-only garnish): inline SVG filter with feImage displacement map (X in R, Y in B, 0.5 neutral), feDisplacementMap scale ~ -70 (negative = concave-lens refraction), region -35%/170%, colorInterpolationFilters=sRGB, applied as filter:url(#id) ON the same element that has backdrop-filter; gate behind engine detection and design the component to read complete without it.

Chromatic aberration recipe: run displacement 3x at scales k, k - a*0.05*|k|, k - a*0.1*|k|; isolate R/G/B via feColorMatrix; recombine with feBlend mode=screen; soften with feGaussianBlur stdDeviation 0.1-0.5.

Edge-only distortion: derive the mask from the displacement map's own luminance (0.3-grayscale feColorMatrix -> feFuncA discrete [0, a*0.05, 1]); composite aberrated edges 'in' the mask over an undisplaced center 'in' the inverted mask — refraction lives at the rim, center stays legible.

Displacement map generation: rounded-rect signed distance field (qx=|x|-w+r, qy=|y|-h+r, min(max(qx,qy),0)+len(max(qx,0),max(qy,0))-r) with smoothstep falloff, encoded as displacement-around-128-gray; pre-bake per corner-radius family as tiny assets rather than shipping 41KB of base64 or running per-pixel JS at runtime.

Elastic pointer physics (optional, JS): activation zone 200px from element edges, linear fade; translate = deltaMouse * elasticity(0.15) * 0.1 * fade; stretch 1 + 0.3*axisAlignment*intensity, squash -0.15 cross-axis, clamp scale >= 0.8; drive via CSS variables + transform, never React/Vue state per mousemove.

Degradation contract: Safari/Firefox tier = blur + saturate + bezel + sheen + shadows (must look finished on its own); Chromium tier adds displacement + aberration. Never let the fallback change layout, color, or perceived quality class — only lose the refraction.
risks: Abandonware: zero commits since 2025-06-13 (~14 months), 24 open issues, obvious fix PRs (#26 Firefox fallback, #27 Tailwind removal) unmerged — no security/compat updates will come.

Published npm artifact is stale: 1.1.1 peer-requires react>=19 even though the repo fixed it to >=18 — and the library is React-only, so it is flatly unusable in this Vue/Nuxt + Tailwind v4 codebase without a full rewrite anyway.

The core refraction relies on unspecified Chromium behavior (CSS filter:url() applied over backdrop-filter output). A Chromium compositor change could silently kill it even in Electron; it already renders nothing in Safari/Firefox.

Safari (the hosted PWA target) never shows displacement or chromatic aberration — any design that depends on refraction for legibility/hierarchy will look broken there; the fallback must be the design baseline.

Performance: 3-pass feDisplacementMap over a backdrop-filtered layer causes reported frame drops (issue #3); per-mousemove framework re-renders and O(w*h) main-thread shader-map generation compound it. In a design system used across many surfaces this multiplies; cap concurrent displacement surfaces and prefer CSS-variable-driven pointer effects.

Layout hijack: the component forces translate(-50%,-50%) centering with 5-7 size-synced absolute sibling layers, sized via getBoundingClientRect + window resize only (no ResizeObserver) — brittle in flex/grid flows and during content-driven resizes (issues #13, #20, #22).

mix-blend-mode screen/overlay layers require a shared stacking context with the page backdrop; ancestors with transform/filter/opacity/isolation (common in Electron app shells and animated routes) will break the bezel and sheen blending.

backdrop-filter itself is expensive on large surfaces and low-end GPUs; Safari also caps/behaves differently with nested backdrop-filters — token defaults should keep blur radii small and surfaces bounded.
SSR/SSG: any port that touches navigator/window at render time (as the original does) crashes Nuxt server rendering — engine detection must be client-only and post-hydration.
Accessibility: refraction, aberration, and elastic motion need prefers-reduced-motion / prefers-reduced-transparency fallbacks — the original ships none.
liquidGlassReact.recommendation: Reimplement the ideas as first-party CSS tokens/utilities with graceful degradation; do not depend on or vendor the package. Depending on it is a non-starter: it is React-only (this is a Vue/Nuxt + Tailwind v4 codebase), effectively unmaintained since June 2025, its published npm artifact ships wrong peer deps, it hijacks layout with forced centering and sibling-layer stacks, requires Tailwind classnames in the host, is SSR-unsafe, and re-renders per mousemove. Vendoring the source inherits all of those design flaws plus 41KB of base64 maps for an effect that must be redesigned to degrade anyway. The valuable IP is small and MIT-licensed: (1) the Chromium quirk of stacking filter:url(#feDisplacementMap-graph) on top of backdrop-filter to refract the backdrop, (2) the edge-masked 3-pass chromatic aberration graph, (3) the mask-composite:exclude double bezel with screen+overlay blending, and (4) the SDF displacement-map math. Build it in three tiers: Tier 0 (all engines, the design baseline) — Tailwind v4 @theme tokens for glass blur/saturation, bezel rings, sheen states, and shadows, all pure CSS, identical in Electron and Safari; Tier 1 (optional JS) — pointer-driven bezel angle and elastic transform written to CSS custom properties via rAF-throttled listeners, honoring prefers-reduced-motion; Tier 2 (Electron/Chromium only) — a small client-only Vue directive/component that injects one shared inline SVG filter (pre-baked SDF maps per radius family, feImage/feDisplacementMap/aberration graph as documented in designRules) and applies filter:url() to the glass substrate, gated by engine detection with a hard budget on concurrent displacement surfaces. Because Safari must look finished at Tier 0, design sign-off should happen against the Safari rendering, with refraction treated strictly as Chromium garnish. This yields a few KB of CSS instead of ~70KB of JS, no dead dependency, and one degradation contract you control.

appleLiquidGlass.summary: Liquid Glass (WWDC 2025) is Apple's cross-platform material that splits every interface into exactly two tiers: an opaque content layer, and a floating functional layer (controls + navigation) rendered in a dynamic glass material. The glass is not simple blur — it is a composite of lensing (light bending at edges), highlight, shadow, and illumination layers, with algorithmic luminance adaptation: over light content the glass lightens and its foreground darkens, and vice versa. Two variants exist: 'regular' (adaptive, self-legible, the default) and 'clear' (permanently translucent, no adaptive behavior, media-only, requires a dimming layer). Apple's own guidance is emphatic that glass never belongs in the content layer, must never stack on other glass, and should be used sparingly on only the most important functional elements. The rollout validated the critics: beta 1–2 drew heavy legibility criticism (NN/g called it 'cracked'), beta 3 frosted much of it over, beta 4 partially restored it, and iOS/macOS 26.1 shipped a user-facing Clear/Tinted opacity toggle — proving that any adoption must build the legibility machinery (scrims, tint floors, vibrancy, accessibility fallbacks) in from day one, not as a patch.
keyFacts: Two-layer model: Liquid Glass forms 'a distinct functional layer for controls and navigation elements — like tab bars and sidebars — that floats above the content layer' (HIG Materials). Content scrolls and peeks through beneath it; the glass layer is where navigation lives, the content layer is where work lives.

Explicit prohibition: 'Don't use Liquid Glass in the content layer' (HIG). Content-layer differentiation uses the standard materials instead (ultra-thin / thin / regular / thick opaque-ish blurs). Sole exception: transient interactive elements (e.g. a slider knob or toggle during drag) momentarily adopt glass to signal interactivity.

Two variants, never mixed: 'regular' blurs and adjusts the luminosity of background content to keep text legible, works at any size over any content, anything can be placed on it — used by most system components and required for text-heavy surfaces (alerts, sidebars, popovers). 'clear' is highly translucent with NO adaptive behaviors, only for components floating over visually rich media (photos/video).

Clear-variant dimming rule with an exact number: if underlying content is bright, add a dark dimming layer at 35% opacity behind clear glass; skip it only when the underlying content is already sufficiently dark (HIG Materials).

Material anatomy (Meet Liquid Glass, WWDC25-219): lensing bends and warps background content at edges rather than scattering it; the material composites highlight (light casting, follows device/pointer motion), shadow (depth separation, deepens over text), and illumination (glow from beneath on interaction) layers.

Legibility mechanics: adaptive tint maps a designer-chosen hue to 'a range of tones mapped to content brightness'; foreground text/symbols use vibrancy levels (default/secondary/tertiary — quaternary too low-contrast on thin materials); scroll edge effect obscures content scrolling under bars, in 'soft' (gradient fade + blur) and 'hard' (uniform band, higher contrast) variants.

Size-dependent behavior: smaller elements are more translucent and dynamic with stronger edge lensing; larger surfaces cast deeper shadows and render more opaque/stable — e.g. a half sheet is translucent, but 'when a half sheet expands to full height, it transitions to a more opaque appearance' (Adopting Liquid Glass).

Motion: controls are gel-like — they stretch, bounce, and morph with springy elasticity; buttons fluidly morph into the menus/popovers they open; action sheets originate from their triggering element, not the screen edge; slider/toggle knobs turn to glass during interaction; custom glass elements are grouped in a GlassEffectContainer so shapes can morph into one another and render in one pass.

Concentric corner radii: hardware curvature informs control shape; nested rounded elements should be concentric with their containers (inner radius = outer radius minus inset), via dedicated concentric-shape APIs; windows/sheets got rounder corners so controls 'nestle into' them.

Accessibility fallbacks are system-automatic for standard components: Reduce Transparency → frosted near-opaque glass; Increase Contrast → foreground pushed toward pure black/white plus borders on controls; Reduce Motion → elastic deformation and morphs disabled. Apple additionally shipped a user-facing Clear vs Tinted (more opaque) Liquid Glass setting in iOS 26.1.

Failure modes Apple was criticized for: variable contrast ratios over arbitrary backdrops (text-over-text, Control Center and Music unreadable in beta 1), glass-on-glass stacking, cramped/unpredictable morphing controls harming discoverability (NN/G: 'Liquid Glass Is Cracked'), motion-as-decoration; mitigations shipped iteratively: beta 3 increased opacity/frosting and bolder tints, beta 4 re-balanced, 26.1 added the opacity toggle.

Performance guidance: glass is GPU-intensive; avoid it in nested views, high-frequency scrollable areas, and lists; reserve it for static top-level chrome (tab bars, toolbars) and combine custom effects in one container.

Primary sources: HIG Materials (developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/materials), Adopting Liquid Glass (developer.apple.com/documentation/technologyoverviews/adopting-liquid-glass), Meet Liquid Glass (developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2025/219/), createwithswift.com/exploring-a-new-visual-language-liquid-glass/, joshcusick.substack.com (legibility-mechanics deep dive), css-tricks.com/getting-clarity-on-apples-liquid-glass/ (web recreation), nngroup.com/articles/liquid-glass/ (usability critique), macrumors.com/2025/10/20/ios-26-1-transparency-option-liquid-glass/ (Clear/Tinted toggle).
designRules: LAYER TOKENS: Define exactly two z-tiers — `layer.content` (editor panes, terminal, chat/agent transcript, diff views, file-tree list rows: always opaque or standard-material backgrounds) and `layer.chrome` (toolbars, activity/tab bars, command palette, floating HUDs, context menus, status pills). Glass utilities are valid ONLY on `layer.chrome` components; a lint rule should reject `glass.*` classes inside content-layer components.

NO GLASS-ON-GLASS: A glass surface may never contain or overlap another glass surface. Popovers/menus opened from a glass control morph out of that control (one continuous surface, one shared backdrop-filter container), never layer a second glass plane over it. Encode: nested `.glass` is a build error; one glass container per control cluster.

MATERIAL TOKENS: `glass.regular` = backdrop blur ~20–30px + saturation boost + luminance-adaptive tint + shadow; the default and the ONLY variant allowed under text (sidebars, palettes, menus, alerts). `glass.clear` = high translucency, no adaptation; permitted solely over rich media (image/video preview panes), never over code or text, and MUST composite a black 35%-opacity dim layer beneath when the media is bright (omit only over already-dark media).

TINT FLOOR / LEGIBILITY FLOOR: `glass.regular` always carries an opaque plate under the blur — e.g. `background: rgba(surfaceColor, ≥0.55–0.65)` in addition to backdrop-filter — so worst-case backdrop still yields ≥4.5:1 for body text and ≥3:1 for large text/icons. Adaptive variant: sample backdrop luminance (or use theme as proxy) and flip foreground between light/dark ink rather than using one fixed gray.

VIBRANCY TOKENS for on-glass foreground: `ink.vibrant.primary` (default, highest contrast), `.secondary`, `.tertiary` for labels/symbols on glass; never use `quaternary`-strength ink on thin/translucent surfaces; separators get one dedicated on-glass separator token.

SCROLL EDGE EFFECT: any glass bar with content scrolling beneath it gets a scrim token — `scrollEdge.soft` (progressive blur + opacity gradient, for sparse content) or `scrollEdge.hard` (uniform higher-opacity band, for dense text like code and lists — the IDE default). Never let raw code/text scroll directly under unscrimmed glass.

ACCENT TINT DISCIPLINE: tinted glass is reserved for the single primary action in a control cluster (e.g. the Run/Send button); tint is defined as a hue that maps to a luminance range, with explicit light, dark, and increased-contrast values per token — never one fixed hex applied over glass. Everything else on chrome stays monochrome so content provides the color.

SIZE-DEPENDENT MATERIAL: scale material params with surface size — small controls (≤ ~44px height: buttons, pills, knobs) get lower plate opacity, stronger edge highlight/lensing, more elastic motion; large panes (sidebars, command palette, sheets) get higher plate opacity, deeper/larger shadow, subtler edge treatment; a surface that expands (palette → full overlay) animates toward opacity as it grows. Encode as size tiers: `glass.sm` / `glass.md` / `glass.lg` with opacity/blur/shadow ramps.

CONCENTRIC RADII: never hand-pick nested corner radii — compute `radius.inner = radius.outer − inset` (clamp ≥ 4px, and cap so it never exceeds the parent's). Provide a `concentric(parentRadius, padding)` utility/CSS custom-property chain; window → panel → control radii all derive from one outer value so corners share centers.

MOTION TOKENS: interaction feedback is springy and morph-based — press = slight scale + illumination glow; button→menu = shape morph from the source element (shared-element transition), not a fade-in at a detached position; use one spring curve token set (e.g. `spring.snappy` for controls, `spring.gentle` for panes). ALL of it gated: `prefers-reduced-motion` replaces morphs with ≤150ms crossfades and kills elastic deformation and any pointer-tracking highlight parallax.

ACCESSIBILITY FALLBACK MATRIX (mandatory, media-query/OS-setting driven): `prefers-reduced-transparency` → swap all `glass.*` to near-opaque frosted tokens (keep hierarchy, kill see-through); `prefers-contrast: more` → push on-glass ink to pure black/white and add 1px hairline borders to glass controls; also ship an in-app user preference mirroring Apple's 26.1 'Clear vs Tinted' toggle that raises the tint floor globally.

PERFORMANCE BUDGET: backdrop-filter is expensive — cap simultaneous glass surfaces on screen (chrome bars + at most one floating overlay), never apply glass per-row in lists or inside high-frequency scroll regions, and give each glass region its own compositing layer (`will-change: backdrop-filter` sparingly). Glass belongs on static top-level chrome only.

CHROME RECEDES: glass chrome may minimize/thin when the user scrolls or focuses content (tab bar shrink on scroll-down, expand on scroll-up), but controls must not appear/disappear unpredictably (the NN/g critique) — position and membership of chrome stay stable; only prominence animates.
risks: A coding-agent IDE is the worst-case content type for glass: nearly every surface is dense text (code, diffs, logs, transcripts). Literal adoption of translucency under/over text areas will reproduce exactly the beta-1 failures (text-over-text, variable contrast) that NN/g documented and Apple had to frost over. Glass must stay confined to chrome.

WCAG compliance becomes probabilistic without a tint floor: translucent surfaces create variable contrast ratios that pass over one backdrop and fail over another (bright markdown preview, light-theme diff). Any token system must guarantee worst-case contrast, not average-case.

Dark, uniform IDE backdrops undercut the premise: Liquid Glass earns its complexity when rich, colorful content shines through. Over a flat dark editor it degrades to 'slightly gray blur' — high implementation cost for near-zero visible payoff — which is also the path to generic glassmorphism AI-slop (blur + white border + transparency with none of the adaptive machinery).

Web/Electron cannot replicate the real material: backdrop-filter gives blur/saturation but not lensing/refraction (needs SVG filter or WebGL hacks with poor cross-browser behavior, notably Safari), and there is no OS-level luminance sampling — adaptive tint must be approximated per-theme or via manual backdrop sampling, which is expensive and fragile.

GPU/compositing cost: multiple large backdrop-filter regions (sidebar + toolbar + palette) can tank frame rates in Electron/Chromium, especially during scroll of the content beneath — Apple itself warns glass is GPU-intensive and bans it from scroll-frequent areas.

Morphing/adaptive chrome erodes IDE predictability: NN/g's strongest critique was controls that appear, vanish, and reflow contextually. Developer tools live on muscle memory; motion and minimization should modulate prominence only, never position or presence of controls.

Apple churned the spec for months (beta 3 frost → beta 4 restore → 26.1 user toggle): treating any single screenshot-era of iOS 26 as the canonical look risks building to a moving target. Build the opacity range (Clear↔Tinted) into tokens so the design can slide along it, as Apple ultimately did.

Accessibility fallbacks are not optional garnish: without reduce-transparency / increase-contrast / reduce-motion pathways designed up front, the glass system has no legal/usable floor for affected users — Apple ships these at the OS level, but a custom web implementation gets none of it for free.
appleLiquidGlass.recommendation: Adopt Liquid Glass as a discipline, not a spectacle. Take the four transferable ideas — (1) strict two-tier layering with glass exclusively on floating chrome (command palette, toolbars, status HUD, context menus, floating action clusters) and fully opaque content panes for code/diffs/transcripts; (2) legibility machinery baked into the tokens: a ≥55–65% tint floor under every blur, vibrancy-tiered ink, hard scroll-edge scrims wherever content scrolls under chrome, and the 35% dim rule if a clear variant is ever used over media; (3) concentric radii derived from one outer radius rather than per-component values; (4) springy morph-from-source motion for chrome, fully gated by reduced-motion/transparency/contrast fallbacks plus an in-app Clear↔Tinted opacity preference mirroring Apple's 26.1 fix. Skip the parts that don't survive contact with an IDE: no clear-variant glass anywhere near text, no lensing/refraction shader theatrics in Electron (a subtle 1px inner highlight + shadow reads as 'glass edge' at a fraction of the cost), no per-row or in-content glass, and no contextually appearing/vanishing controls. Concretely: encode `layer.content` vs `layer.chrome`, `glass.regular` in three size tiers, vibrancy ink tokens, scroll-edge scrim tokens, a concentric-radius utility, one spring token pair, and the three accessibility override maps — and enforce 'no glass in content, no glass on glass' with lint rules so the system cannot regress into glassmorphism slop.
